title: Tumbling Window
explain: A tumbling window cuts time into fixed-size, non-overlapping, back-to-back intervals, so every event belongs to exactly one window. It is the natural unit for counters and totals per period, like requests per minute. Its blind spot is the boundary, and its common problem is data skew, which I fix with two layers of windows using salting.
model:
Windows `[start1, end1), [start2, end2), ...`: independent (own state, no overlap) yet contiguous (no gaps). Assignment: `window_start = ts - (ts mod size)`. Per window you keep only the aggregate, emit it at close and drop the state.

Settle two things:

- **Which clock?** Event time is correct but needs a **watermark** to decide a window is complete and a late-data policy (drop, allow lateness, emit a correction). Processing time is simple but shifts with delays.
- **Boundary effect.** 100 events at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:01 look like two calm minutes. A 'max 100 per minute' tumbling counter can admit 200 in 2 seconds. For 'any 60 seconds' use a [sliding window](#/sd/f/sliding-window-aggregation).

**Data skew** (user's phrase: 旱的旱死, 涝的涝死, the drought kills the dry, the flood drowns the wet): one hot key lands on one worker. Fix with **two layers of tumbling windows**, divide and conquer ([salting](#/sd/f/salting)):

```
layer 1 key = item_123_<random 0..7>  -> partial counts spread across workers
layer 2 key = item_123  (salt stripped) -> merge partials per original key and window
```

Works for mergeable aggregates (count, sum, max), not exact medians.

details.q: Tumbling windows are 5 minutes wide, aligned to :00. Which window holds an event at 12:07:42?
details.a: [12:05:00, 12:10:00). window_start = ts - (ts mod size), and the end is exclusive, so a boundary event belongs to the later window.

details.q: A rule says at most 100 requests per minute, enforced with a per-minute tumbling counter. What is the worst case in a 2 s span?
details.a: 200: 100 just before the boundary and 100 just after, each minute's counter staying at its limit. This is why tumbling windows suit reporting, while rate limits needing 'any 60 s' use a sliding window.

Event time is correct, because results do not depend on delivery delay, but you need a watermark to know when a window is complete. Processing time is simpler and fine when approximate counts are acceptable.

details.q: A window was emitted when the watermark passed 12:01:05, and at 12:02 an event stamped 12:00:30 arrives. What do you do?
details.a: Apply the lateness policy: drop and count it as late, or, if within allowed lateness, emit a corrected result for [12:00, 12:01) that downstream treats as an update. Never silently add it to the open window by arrival time.

details.q: A hot key makes up most of the traffic in a windowed count. What is the fix?
details.a: Two layers. Layer 1 keys by original key plus a random salt so the hot key spreads over workers and each computes a partial. Layer 2 strips the salt and merges partials per original key and window. It only works for mergeable aggregates.

details.q: Why not salt in only one layer?
details.a: The salted partials need a second merge step to give the true per-key total. Without layer 2, consumers would have to sum results themselves.

prompts.q: Explain tumbling windows and when you would choose them.
points: Each event in exactly one window
Good for per-period counters and reports

prompts.q: Explain the boundary effect and event-time pitfalls.
points: Events straddling the edge look calm in both windows
Rate limiting or alerting needs a sliding window
Late events: drop, allow lateness, or emit a correction

prompts.q: Describe how to handle a hot key in a windowed aggregation.
points: Data skew sends one key to one worker
Layer 1: salt the key randomly to spread partials
Layer 2: strip salt and merge per key and window
